title: Testing materials: which one is best for the job?

summary.text: A rubber band and a strip of milk packet can both be stretched. Only one of them goes back to its old length when you let go. You cannot find this out by looking. You have to test. In this unit you hang a water bottle from strips of rubber, cloth and paper, and measure how much each one stretches. You also find out which materials keep water out, and which are strong enough to lift a bottle.
summary.art: A broom handle resting across the backs of two chairs, with a rubber band, a T-shirt strip, a hanky strip and a newspaper strip hanging from it, and a child holding a ruler beside them.

intro.hook: Hold a rubber band in one hand and a strip of an old milk packet in the other. Pull both gently. Both get longer. Now let go. What happens to each one?
intro.text: The rubber band snaps back. The milk packet strip stays long and thin. Both looked like soft, bendy things before you pulled them. A material can surprise you, so scientists test it. A test means doing something to a material on purpose and watching what happens. Before you read on, guess. Which material in your home stretches the most? You are going to find out.
intro.art: A child's two hands, one letting go of a rubber band that springs back short, the other holding a long, thin, white strip of milk packet that has stayed stretched.

outcomes: By the end I can test which material stretches the most, by hanging the same weight from each one and measuring.
By the end I can say if a stretched material springs back or stays stretched.
By the end I can test which materials are waterproof and which are absorbent.
By the end I can test which material is strongest by seeing how much it can lift before it tears.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, and then say what my test showed.
By the end I can choose a material for a job and say which test tells me it is right.

terms.meaning: What a thing is made of. Rubber, cotton, paper, plastic, steel and wood are materials.
terms.example: A hair band is made of rubber and cloth. A tumbler is made of steel.
terms.art: A hair band, a steel tumbler and a wooden spoon, each with a label for its material.

terms.meaning: Doing something to a material on purpose, and watching or measuring what happens.
terms.example: Hanging a water bottle from a strip, and measuring how long the strip gets, is a stretch test.
terms.art: A child hanging a water bottle from a strip of cloth and holding a ruler beside it.

terms.meaning: Gets longer when you pull it, without breaking.
terms.example: A rubber band and the top of a sock are stretchy. A strip of newspaper is not.
terms.art: A rubber band being pulled long between two fingers.

terms.meaning: Goes back to its old shape after you stop pulling or pressing.
terms.example: A rubber band is elastic. The skin on the back of your hand is elastic too.
terms.art: A rubber band before, pulled long, and back to its old size, in three small pictures.

terms.example: A raincoat, a polythene sheet and a banana leaf are waterproof.
terms.art: Water drops sitting as round beads on a banana leaf.

terms.example: A towel, a paper napkin and a sponge are absorbent.
terms.art: A paper napkin soaking up a spill, with the wet patch spreading.

terms.meaning: Hard to break or tear. A strong material can hold a big weight.
terms.example: A strip of cotton cloth can lift a full water bottle. A strip of paper napkin tears.
terms.art: A strip of cloth holding up a full water bottle, and a torn strip of napkin beside it.

terms.meaning: To say what you think will happen, before you test it, and why.
terms.example: 'I predict the rubber band will stretch the most, because it is bendy.'
terms.art: A child with a thinking bubble showing a long rubber band.

explanations.context: This card explains why scientists test materials instead of only looking at them.
explanations.definition: A test is doing something to a material on purpose and seeing what happens. It shows what a material does, which looking alone cannot show.
explanations.description: A thick cotton towel looks as if it would keep rain out, but water soaks into it. A thin sheet of polythene looks weak, but it keeps water out completely. So we cannot always tell by looking. We test. In a fair test every material gets the same bottle, the same water and the same time, so only the material is different.
examples: Stretch test: the same full bottle hangs from every strip.
Waterproof test: the same spoon of water goes on every square.
Strength test: every strip is the same size, and water is added to the bottle one cup at a time.
explanations.art: A child looking at a thick wool square and a thin polythene square, with a thinking bubble asking which one keeps water out.

explanations.concept: Stretchy and elastic: why a rubber band springs back
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the stretch test: why the rubber band went back to its old length, and the milk packet strip did not.
explanations.definition: A stretchy material gets longer when it is pulled. An elastic material goes back to its old length when the pull stops.
explanations.description: Everything is made of tiny particles, far too small to see. In rubber, the particles are joined in very long chains, curled up like a heap of loose thread. Pulling straightens the chains, and letting go lets them curl up again, so the rubber goes back. In a milk packet, the plastic chains slide to new places when you pull, and they stay there. Pull rubber too far, and the chains break and the band snaps.
examples: A rubber band, a hair band, the top of a sock and the skin on your hand are elastic.
A strip of milk packet and a roll of atta dough stretch, but stay stretched.
A strip of newspaper hardly stretches at all. Pull hard, and it tears.
explanations.art: A zoom-in picture: a rubber band with a circle showing tangled, curled chains inside, and beside it the same band stretched, with the chains pulled straight.

explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the waterproof test: why water went through some squares and stayed on top of others.
explanations.definition: A waterproof material does not let water through. An absorbent material soaks water up.
explanations.description: Paper and cotton are made of tiny fibres, like very thin threads, with tiny gaps between them. Water creeps into the gaps and spreads along the fibres, so it soaks in and goes through. Polythene and foil have no gaps, so water stays on top as a round drop. A banana leaf also has a thin layer of wax, and water slides off wax.
examples: Waterproof: a polythene sheet, foil, a steel plate, a banana leaf, an umbrella.
Absorbent: a towel, a paper napkin, newspaper, a cotton hanky, a sponge.
A raincoat must be waterproof. A towel must be absorbent. Each one is right for its own job.
explanations.art: Two zoom-in circles: one showing water creeping between paper fibres, one showing a round drop sitting on a smooth polythene surface.

explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the bottle lift test: why some strips held the bottle and some tore.
explanations.definition: A strong material is hard to break or tear. It can hold a big weight. A weak material breaks or tears with a small weight.
explanations.description: In cotton cloth, the threads are twisted and woven tightly, so they hold on to each other well. A paper napkin is made of short fibres pressed loosely together, so a small pull drags them apart. Strong is not always best: a napkin is useful because it is soft and absorbent, not because it is strong.
examples: Strong: cotton cloth, rope, a thick carry bag, steel.
Weak: a paper napkin, toilet paper, a dry leaf.
Wet paper is weaker than dry paper, because water loosens its fibres.
explanations.art: A zoom-in of woven cotton threads crossing over and under each other, next to a zoom-in of loose, short paper fibres.

explanations.concept: Is the best material always the strongest one?
explanations.context: This card is about choosing a material for a job, where people can sensibly disagree.
explanations.description: There is often no one best material. It depends on the job, and on what matters most to the person choosing.
examples: A cloth bag is strong and can be used for years. A paper bag is weaker but rots away quickly if it is thrown out.
A steel tiffin box is strong. A banana leaf is waterproof, free in many places, and goes back into the soil.

perspectives.explanation: The best bag is the cheapest one that does not tear on the way home.

perspectives.who: A person who cares most about the Earth
perspectives.explanation: The best bag is one you use again and again, like a cloth bag, even if it costs more at first.
First say exactly what the job needs: how much weight, how wet, how long. Then test, and pick the material that passes.

explanations.art: A cloth bag, a paper bag and a polythene bag in a row, each with a question mark above.

agreed.text: You often cannot tell what a material can do just by looking at it. You have to test it.
agreed.evidence: A thick towel looks as if it could stop water, but water soaks into it. Thin polythene looks weak, but it keeps water out. Tests show both.

agreed.text: Rubber is elastic because it is made of very long, curled-up chains of tiny particles.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have studied the long chains with special tools. When rubber is stretched, the chains line up, and X-rays have shown this.

agreed.text: Most paper is absorbent because it is made of tiny plant fibres with gaps between them.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, paper looks like a flat mat of tiny threads. Water creeps along them and fills the gaps.

challenging.claim: A thicker cloth always keeps out more water.
challenging.for: Thick cloth has more material for the water to get through, so it can slow the water down.
challenging.against: A thick towel soaks up water and lets it through. A thin polythene sheet or an umbrella cloth keeps it out. What matters most is whether the material has gaps, not how thick it is.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess many children make in the waterproof test.

challenging.claim: Natural materials are always weaker than materials made in factories.
challenging.for: Steel and nylon rope are very strong. Many natural things, like leaves and paper napkins, tear easily.
challenging.against: Some natural materials are very strong. Coir rope made from coconut fibre holds boats. Weight for weight, the silk that spiders use for their safety line is stronger than steel.
challenging.context: This card is about whether natural or made materials are stronger.

challenging.claim: If a material stretches, it will always spring back.
challenging.for: Rubber bands, hair bands and socks stretch and spring back, and these are the stretchy things we use most.
challenging.against: A strip of milk packet and a roll of atta dough stretch and stay stretched. Even a rubber band stays a little longer if it is stretched too far for too long.
challenging.context: This card is about what you saw in the stretch test.

big_questions.q: Why did the rubber band go back, but the milk packet strip stayed long?
big_questions.hint: Think of the tiny chains inside. Did they curl up again, or slide to new places?

big_questions.q: How many tests do you need before you really know a material?
big_questions.hint: We tested stretching, keeping water out and lifting. Is there anything else a material can do?

big_questions.q: Your skin stretches when you bend your knee, and goes back. What other parts of you are elastic?
big_questions.hint: Think of your ears, your lips, the inside of your cheek.

big_questions.q: Is there a best material in the whole world?
big_questions.hint: Is the best raincoat material also the best towel?

big_questions.q: A rubber tree makes latex. Why might the tree need a stretchy, sticky material?
big_questions.hint: Latex flows out where the bark is cut. What could it do there?

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many people in Europe and America believed that useful rubber was invented in 1839. Raw rubber went sticky in summer and hard and cracked in winter. In 1839, an American named Charles Goodyear heated rubber with sulfur. It stayed stretchy in heat and cold. But people in Mexico and Central America had made bouncy, long-lasting rubber more than 3,000 years before that. The Olmec, Maya and Aztec peoples made rubber balls for a ball game. In the 1990s, Dorothy Hosler, an archaeologist at MIT in the USA, wanted to know how. With her students, she collected milky latex from the Castilla rubber tree. They mixed it with juice from a morning glory vine. The mixture became rubber that was much bouncier and stronger than dried latex alone. Later, Hosler and Michael Tarkanian found that different amounts of vine juice made different rubbers: some best for bouncing balls, some best for tough sandal soles. The old rubber makers had been testing materials to fit each job.
how_we_found_out.who: The Olmec, Maya and Aztec rubber makers; Charles Goodyear (1839); Dorothy Hosler, with Sandra Burkett and Michael Tarkanian (1999)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That useful, lasting rubber was first made by Charles Goodyear in 1839. Hosler's team showed that the peoples of ancient Mexico had made it more than 3,000 years earlier, by mixing latex with morning glory juice.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist in a field in Mexico pouring white latex into a bowl of green vine juice, with an old-style rubber ball beside her.

story.title: The Band That Came Back
story.note: Rubber trees (Hevea brasiliensis) are grown widely in Kerala, especially around Kottayam. Tappers cut a thin slanting groove in the bark early in the morning, and white latex drips into a cup. Latex left on skin dries into a thin rubbery film. Meenu, Susheela and Joseph are made up.
text: Meenu was seven. In the school holidays, she went to stay with her aunt Susheela in a village near Kottayam, in Kerala. Behind the house grew rows and rows of tall rubber trees.
Her cousin Joseph was there too. He was nine, and he liked to say he knew everything.
On the first morning, Meenu's hair band broke. It was an old one. When she pulled it, it did not spring back. It just stayed long and loose, and then it snapped.
"Your band is finished," said Joseph. "Rubber gets old. Throw it away."
Meenu held the two broken ends. "Why did it stop springing back?" she asked.
Aunt Susheela laughed. "Come with me early tomorrow," she said. "I will show you where rubber comes from."

The next morning it was still dark and cool. Aunt Susheela took a small curved knife and a torch. They walked between the rubber trees. Each tree had a slanting line cut in the bark, and a coconut-shell cup tied below it.
Aunt Susheela shaved a very thin strip of bark off the line. Slowly, white drops came out. They ran down the groove and dripped into the cup.
"That is latex," said Aunt Susheela. "The tree makes latex to seal a cut, the way your blood seals a cut on your knee. We take a little each morning."

Meenu touched a drop. It was cool and sticky. She rubbed it between her finger and thumb. After a while, the white had turned into a thin, clear skin. She pulled at it. It stretched. She let go. It sprang back.
"It is rubber already!" said Meenu.
"Of course," said Joseph. "Everything soft is stretchy. Look." He picked up a piece of the polythene sheet that covered the firewood. He pulled it. It got longer.
"But does it come back?" asked Meenu.
Joseph let go. The polythene stayed long. It had gone thin and white in the middle. It did not come back at all.
Joseph frowned. "That is the same thing," he said. "It stretched."
"No," said Meenu. "The rubber stretched and came back. Your plastic stretched and stayed. They are different. We have to test them properly."

Back at the house, Meenu found a ball of string, a ruler and an old water bottle. She filled the bottle with water. She tied a piece of new rubber band, a strip of polythene and a strip of cotton from an old towel to the window bars, one beside the other.
"Every one gets the same bottle," she said. "Then it is fair."
She hung the bottle on the rubber band. The band stretched long, nearly double. Joseph measured it with the ruler. She took the bottle off. The band went back to its old length.
Then the polythene strip. It stretched a little and stayed a little longer. Then the cotton strip. It hardly moved at all.
"So the cotton is strongest and not stretchy," said Joseph slowly. "The rubber band is stretchy and comes back. The polythene stretches and stays."
"Now you know three things," said Aunt Susheela. "And you did not guess them. You tested them."
Meenu looked at her old hair band. "So why did my band stop coming back?"
"Rubber that is very old, or left in the hot sun, changes," said Aunt Susheela. "Sunlight and air slowly break the long chains inside it. Then it cannot spring back, and it snaps."
Meenu thought about the trees, making their latex every morning, sealing their cuts. She thought about her band, slowly getting old.
That evening she wrote in her notebook: "Do not believe it. Test it." Joseph read it over her shoulder. For once, he did not say he knew already.
story.epiphany: Two materials can both stretch and still be very different. You only find out what a material does by testing it.
ask: What did the rubber do that the polythene did not?
How did Meenu make her test fair?
Why did Aunt Susheela say the old hair band snapped?
art: Before dawn in a rubber plantation in Kerala, a woman with a torch cuts a thin line in the bark, and white latex drips into a coconut-shell cup while a girl watches.
A girl and a boy at a window with bars, a rubber band, a polythene strip and a cotton strip hanging side by side, and a water bottle on the rubber band.

experiments.title: The Stretch Test: which material stretches the most?
experiments.context: In this experiment you hang the same full water bottle from a rubber band and from strips of T-shirt, hanky and newspaper. You measure how much longer each one gets. Then you take the bottle off and see which ones come back.
experiments.question: Which material stretches the most when the same bottle hangs from it? And when the bottle comes off, which ones go back to their old length?
experiments.predict: Pull each strip gently with your fingers. Then put them in a line, from the one you think will stretch the most to the one that will stretch the least. Why did you put your first one first?
experiments.fair_test: Every strip gets the same full bottle, hung the same way. Each strip is 2 cm wide. We wait the same time, 10 seconds, before we measure. We use the same ruler, and measure from the broom handle to the paper clip every time. The rubber band is not 2 cm wide and starts shorter than the strips, so we compare how many centimetres longer each one gets.
results_table: Length after the bottle comes off (cm)

materials.item: an ordinary rubber band
a strip of an old cotton T-shirt or banian, 2 cm wide and 16 cm long, cut across the T-shirt from side to side
a strip of an old cotton hanky or dupatta, 2 cm wide and 16 cm long
a strip of newspaper, 2 cm wide and 16 cm long
a strip of a clean, empty milk packet or bread packet, 1 cm wide and about 10 cm long
a half-litre plastic water bottle, full of water, with its cap on
a piece of string, about 30 cm long, to tie a loop round the bottle neck
4 paper clips
sticky tape
a broom or mop handle, or a long stick, and two chairs
a ruler with centimetres
scissors, for the grown-up
a cushion or folded towel, to go on the floor under the bottle

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the strips. Lower the bottle gently, and keep feet away from under it, because a strip may tear. Keep faces away from a stretched rubber band.

schedule.what: Pull and guess. Hang the four strips. Measure each before, with the bottle and after. Pull the milk packet strip. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Write your guess and your reason at the top. Fill in the results table. Draw each strip before and with the bottle. Circle the ones that came back.

setup.art: Two chairs back to back, about half a metre apart, with a broom handle resting across their tops.
setup.caption: 1. Rest a broom handle across two chair backs.

setup.art: A rubber band, a T-shirt strip, a hanky strip and a newspaper strip hanging side by side from the broom handle, each with a paper clip at the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Hang the four strips. Measure each one.

setup.art: A full half-litre water bottle hanging by a string loop from the rubber band, which has stretched long, and a child holding a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Hang the bottle on each strip. Measure again.

setup.art: The rubber band back at its old length, and a child's hands pulling a strip of milk packet that stays long and thin.
setup.caption: 4. Take the bottle off. Did it come back?

flow.do: 1. Lay out the rubber band and the three strips. 2. Let your child pull each one gently with their fingers. 3. Ask the question below. 4. Write down their order and their reason, word for word.
flow.say: Pull each one gently. Which one will stretch the most when a heavy bottle hangs from it? Put them in a line. Why did you put that one first?
flow.kid: Pull each one gently. Which will stretch the most? Put them in a line. Say why.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: The rubber band, because it got long when I pulled it.
The T-shirt, because my T-shirt stretches when I put it on.
The newspaper will stretch least, because paper tears.

flow.parent: Don't say if the guess is right. Any guess with a reason is good. The test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the stretch test. You feel four materials and guess which will stretch the most.

flow.do: 1. Put two chairs back to back, about half a metre apart. 2. Rest a broom handle across the tops. 3. Wrap the top of each strip once round the handle, and tape it to itself. 4. Hang the rubber band over the handle. 5. Fold the bottom of each strip over a paper clip and tape it. Hook a clip through the rubber band too. 6. Tie the string round the bottle neck to make a loop. 7. Put the cushion on the floor below.
flow.say: We hang every strip from the same handle, the same way. Then only the material is different.
flow.kid: Help hang the four strips on the handle. Put the cushion underneath.
flow.parent: Cut the T-shirt strip across the shirt, from one side seam towards the other. Knitted cloth stretches more that way. Keep the strips spaced so they don't touch. The bottle should hang well above the cushion. Tape the ends of the broom handle to the chairs so it cannot roll.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ruler beside the rubber band, with 0 at the top of the handle. 2. Read the length to the paper clip. 3. Write it in the table. 4. Do the same for each strip.
flow.say: First we measure each one with nothing on it. Then we can see how much it changes.
flow.kid: Measure each one from the handle to the clip. Write it down.
flow.parent: The strips should be about 10 cm. The rubber band will be about 6 cm. Small differences are fine. We look at how much longer each one gets.

flow.do: 1. Hook the bottle's string loop onto the rubber band's paper clip. 2. Lower the bottle slowly with your hand under it. 3. Let go, and count to 10. 4. Measure the length again and write it down. 5. Lift the bottle off. 6. Do the same for each strip.
flow.say: Lower it slowly. Count to ten. Now measure. How long is it with the bottle?
flow.kid: Lower the bottle slowly. Count to ten. Measure again. Write it down.

good: The rubber band got much longer.
The T-shirt strip stretched a bit.
The newspaper did not change at all.

flow.parent: Usually the rubber band stretches the most, and the T-shirt strip comes next. The hanky and the newspaper hardly change. If a strip tears, that is a result too: write 'tore'.

check.q: Why do we hang the same bottle on every strip?
options: So the test is fair, and only the material is different
Because we have only one bottle
So the bottle does not fall
check.why: If one strip had a heavier bottle, it might stretch more just because of the bottle. With the same bottle, any difference comes from the material.

flow.do: 1. After you take the bottle off each strip, count to 10. 2. Measure the length again. 3. Write it in the last column. 4. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Now the bottle is off. Did each one go back to its old length?
flow.kid: Take the bottle off. Count to ten. Measure again. Did it come back?

good: The rubber band went back to its old length.
The T-shirt strip came back most of the way, but stayed a little longer.

flow.parent: The rubber band usually goes back to its old length, or within a few millimetres. A knitted T-shirt strip often stays a little longer, about 1 cm.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the milk packet strip. 2. Ask them to pull it slowly with both hands until it gets longer. 3. Let go. 4. Do the same with the rubber band.
flow.say: Pull the milk packet strip slowly until it gets longer. Now let go. What happened? Now try the rubber band.
flow.kid: Pull the milk packet strip slowly. Let go. Now pull the rubber band. Let go. What is different?

ask.q: What did the milk packet strip do?
good: It stayed long and thin.
It went white in the middle and did not come back.

flow.parent: Pull slowly, not with a jerk. A thin milk packet strip gets thin and white in the middle, and stays long. A thick carry bag may be too strong to stretch by hand, so use a milk packet or bread packet.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why. 2. Then read them the card 'Stretchy and elastic: why a rubber band springs back'.
flow.say: So, which material is the stretchiest? What did you see that tells you? And why do you think the rubber band came back, but the milk packet did not?
flow.kid: Which one stretched most? What did you see? Why did the band come back?

ask.q: Why do you think the rubber band came back?
good: Because rubber is elastic.
Because something inside the rubber pulls it back.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the numbers: 'The rubber band got 7 cm longer, more than any other. When the bottle came off, it went back to 6 cm.' Only explain the curled chains after your child has had their say.

experiments.title: The Spot Test: which materials keep water out?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put six squares of different materials over paper marked with sketch pen. You pour the same water on each one, wait, and lift it up. If the sketch pen circle has run, water got through.
experiments.question: Which of these materials are waterproof, and which let water through?
experiments.predict: Feel each square. Which ones do you think will keep the water out? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every square is the same size. Every square gets one level teaspoon of water, poured in the middle, one after the other. We lift all of them after the same 2 minutes. The papers underneath are all the same, with the same kind of sketch pen circle.
results_table: Did the water stay on top or soak in?
Did the circle under it run?

materials.item: squares about 8 cm by 8 cm of: newspaper, a paper napkin, an old cotton hanky, a clean milk packet, kitchen foil, and a banana leaf or cabbage leaf
6 small pieces of white paper, each with a circle drawn in sketch pen
a water-based sketch pen (not a ball pen or a permanent marker)
a teaspoon and a cup of water
a tray or a steel plate
a clock or phone, to time 2 minutes

schedule.what: Draw circles and set out the squares. Guess. Pour water on each. Wait 2 minutes. Lift and look. Sort into waterproof and not waterproof.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Stick the six papers in your notebook, in two groups: dry and wet. Write the name of the material next to each.

setup.art: Six squares in a row on a tray: newspaper, a paper napkin, a cotton hanky, a piece of milk packet, foil and a piece of banana leaf, each on top of a small white paper with a sketch pen circle.
setup.caption: 1. Put each square on a paper with a sketch pen circle.

setup.art: A child pouring a teaspoon of water onto the middle of a square of newspaper.
setup.caption: 2. Pour one teaspoon of water on each square.

setup.art: A child lifting a square of foil to show a clean, dry circle underneath, and beside it a lifted newspaper square showing a blurred, wet circle.
setup.caption: 3. Wait 2 minutes. Lift each square. Did the circle run?

flow.do: 1. Help your child draw a circle with a sketch pen on each of the six papers. 2. Lay the papers on a tray. 3. Put one square of material on each paper.
flow.say: If water gets through a square, it will wet the paper and make the sketch pen run. That is how we will know.
flow.kid: Draw a circle on each paper. Put one square on each.
flow.parent: Water-based sketch pens run when wet, so a wet paper is easy to see. Do not use a ball pen or a permanent marker. If you have no banana leaf, a cabbage leaf from the market works.

flow.do: 1. Let your child feel each square. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Write their guess for each one in the table.
flow.say: Which squares will keep the water out? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Feel each square. Which will keep the water out? Why?

good: The foil is shiny and smooth, so water will stay on top.
The hanky is cloth, and water goes into my clothes in the rain.
The napkin will soak it up, because we use napkins to wipe spills.

flow.parent: Don't correct the guesses. Many children think thick things keep water out. The test will show them.

flow.do: 1. Pour one level teaspoon of water slowly onto the middle of each square, one after the other. 2. Watch the water on each one. 3. Start the clock after you pour the last square.
flow.say: Watch the water. On which squares does the water sit on top as a round drop? On which does it soak in?
flow.kid: Pour one spoon of water on each square. Watch. Does it soak in or stay on top?

ask.q: What is the water doing on the foil?
good: It stays in a round drop.
It sits on top and rolls.

flow.parent: On the napkin and newspaper the water soaks in at once. On the hanky it soaks in more slowly. On foil, milk packet and leaf it sits as a drop.

flow.do: 1. Wait 2 minutes. 2. Lift each square carefully, without tipping its water onto the paper. 3. Look at the circle underneath. 4. Write what you see.
flow.say: Now lift each one carefully. Look at the circle. Did the water get through?
flow.kid: Lift each square slowly. Look at the circle. Is it dry or has it run?

good: Under the foil, the milk packet and the leaf.
The circles under the newspaper, napkin and hanky have run.

flow.parent: Tip the water off the waterproof squares into the tray first, so it does not drip onto the paper as you lift. If a circle is only a little damp, count it as wet: water got through.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to sort the squares into two heaps: waterproof and not waterproof. 2. Ask what they saw and why. 3. Then read the card 'Waterproof and absorbent'.
flow.say: Sort them into two heaps. Which keep water out? Which let it through? Was your guess right? Why do you think the water got through the hanky?
flow.kid: Make two heaps: waterproof and not waterproof. Was your guess right?

ask.q: Why did water get through the hanky?
good: Because cloth has tiny gaps.
Because cotton soaks up water and passes it on.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses what your child saw: 'The circle under the foil stayed dry, so foil is waterproof.'

check.q: Thara, a girl in Class 2, wants to keep her notebook dry on a rainy walk to school. What should she wrap it in?
check.why: In the spot test, water stayed on top of the milk packet and the circle under it stayed dry. The napkin and the hanky soaked the water up and let it through.

activities.title: Stretch and Let Go: a home hunt
activities.context: In this activity you hunt at home for things that stretch. You pull each one gently and let go, then sort them: springs back, stays stretched, or does not stretch.

materials.item: things from home: a hair band, a sock, a pyjama waistband, a balloon if you have one, a small ball of atta dough or clay, a strip of milk packet, a dry leaf, a sheet of paper
three sheets of paper labelled 'Springs back', 'Stays stretched' and 'Does not stretch'

schedule.what: Find things that might stretch. Pull and let go. Sort them into three groups.

activities.record: Draw each thing on the sheet where it belongs.

setup.art: Three labelled sheets on the floor: springs back, stays stretched, does not stretch, with a sock, a hair band and a ball of dough beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out three sheets.

setup.art: A child gently pulling a roll of atta dough that stays long, and a sock top that springs back.
setup.caption: 2. Pull each thing gently. Let go. Put it on a sheet.

setup.art: A child pinching the skin on the back of their hand, and the skin going flat again.
setup.caption: 3. Test your own skin too.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the three sheets. 2. Go round the home with your child and collect 8 to 10 things that might stretch.
flow.say: Let's find things that might stretch. Look in the cupboard, the kitchen and the bathroom.
flow.kid: Find things that might stretch. Bring them here.
flow.parent: Roll a small piece of atta dough into a snake. Clay or play dough works too.

flow.do: 1. Pull each thing gently with both hands. 2. Let go. 3. Put it on the right sheet.
flow.say: Pull gently. Let go. Did it spring back, stay stretched, or not stretch at all?
flow.kid: Pull gently. Let go. Which sheet does it go on?

good: Stays stretched, because it got long and stayed long.

flow.parent: Pull gently. We are testing, not breaking. The sock top and the hair band spring back. The dough and the milk packet stay stretched. The paper and the dry leaf tear instead of stretching.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to pinch the skin on the back of their hand and let go. 2. Watch it go flat. 3. Ask which sheet their skin belongs on.
flow.say: Pinch the skin on the back of your hand. Let go. What happened? Which sheet does your skin go on?
flow.kid: Pinch the skin on your hand. Let go. Watch it go flat. Which sheet?

good: Yes, it springs back.
Yes, it goes flat again.

flow.parent: Skin is elastic, so it springs back. A grandparent's skin goes back more slowly, because skin becomes less elastic with age. Humans and other animals have elastic skin, so they can bend and move.

activities.title: The Bottle Lift: which strip is strongest?
activities.context: In this activity you hang an empty bottle from strips of paper napkin, newspaper, polythene bag and cotton cloth. You pour water into the bottle, one small cup at a time, until the strip tears or the bottle is full.

materials.item: strips 1 cm wide and 16 cm long of: one layer of a paper napkin, newspaper, a thick carry bag (the kind shops give for groceries), and old cotton cloth
an empty half-litre plastic bottle with a string loop tied round its neck
a small cup that holds about 50 ml, and a jug of water (a small katori filled about one-third full is roughly 50 ml; any small cup is fine if you use the same one every time)
the broom handle and two chairs from the stretch test, paper clips and sticky tape
a bucket or a big bowl, to go under the bottle

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the strips. Keep feet and hands away from under the bottle.

schedule.what: Guess. Hang each strip in turn. Add water one cup at a time. Count the cups until it tears.

activities.record: A table: material, my guess, number of cups when it tore (or 'held the full bottle').

setup.art: A strip of paper napkin hanging from a broom handle, with an empty bottle on a string below it and a bucket on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the empty bottle from one strip.

setup.art: A child pouring a small cup of water into the hanging bottle.
setup.caption: 2. Add one cup of water at a time. Count.

setup.art: A torn napkin strip and a bottle resting in a bucket.
setup.caption: 3. Stop when it tears. Write the number of cups.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the four strips. 2. Ask them to guess which will hold the most water, and why.
flow.say: Which strip do you think will lift the most water before it tears? Why?
flow.kid: Which strip will hold the most water? Why do you think so?

good: The cloth, because my clothes don't tear.
The napkin will tear first, because it is thin.

flow.do: 1. Tape one strip to the broom handle and fold a paper clip into the bottom. 2. Hang the empty bottle on it, over the bucket. 3. Pour in one cup of water. Wait 5 seconds. 4. Keep adding one cup at a time, and count. 5. Stop when it tears or the bottle is full. 6. Do the same for each strip.
flow.say: One cup at a time. Count with me. Each strip gets the same bottle and the same cups.
flow.kid: Pour in one cup. Count. Wait. Pour another. Stop when it tears.
flow.parent: The napkin usually tears after only a few cups, often at the tape or the clip. The newspaper, carry bag and cloth may all hold the full bottle. If they do, write 'held the full bottle'. That shows they are much stronger than the napkin. The carry bag may stretch a lot instead of tearing, and the bottle may sink into the bucket. Write 'stretched a lot'. That is a result too.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask which strip was strongest, and how you know.
flow.say: Which strip was strongest? How do you know? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Which strip was strongest? How do you know?

good: The cloth held the full bottle, and the napkin tore after 3 cups.

flow.parent: Read the card 'Strong and weak' after your child has answered.

activities.title: Pick the Material: the right one for the job
activities.context: In this activity you use what you found in your tests to choose a material for six new jobs, and say which test tells you it is right.

materials.item: your results tables from the stretch test, the spot test and the bottle lift
paper and colours

schedule.what: Choose a material for six jobs. Say which test shows it is right.

activities.record: Draw each job with the material you chose. Write the test that helped you.

setup.art: Six small pictures on a page: a shower curtain, a dishcloth, a strap to carry a full water bottle, a pyjama waistband, a cover to keep a school book dry in the rain, and a rope to pull up a bucket from a well.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the six jobs.

setup.art: A child drawing a shower curtain and writing 'milk packet: spot test' beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Choose a material. Name the test.

flow.do: 1. Read each job to your child. 2. The six jobs are: a shower curtain. A dishcloth. A strap to carry a full water bottle. A pyjama waistband. A cover to keep a school book dry in the rain. A rope to pull up a bucket from a well. 3. For each one, ask which material from your tests they would use. 4. Ask which test told them.
flow.say: For a shower curtain, which material would you choose? Which of our tests tells you it is right?
flow.kid: Pick a material for each job. Which test helps you choose?

ask.q: Which material for a dishcloth? Which test?
good: Cotton, because it soaked up the water in the spot test.
A napkin is absorbent too, but it tore in the bottle lift.

flow.parent: There is often more than one good answer. A strong answer names the property the job needs, and the test that showed it.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw two of the jobs with their chosen materials.
flow.say: Draw two of the jobs. Write the material and the test next to each one.
flow.kid: Draw two jobs. Write the material and the test.
flow.parent: Spelling does not matter. You can write the words for your child if they ask.

games.title: The Right Material for the Job
games.context: This is a card game about choosing materials. A job card is turned over, every player points to the material they would use, and you say why.

items.b: Needs to be waterproof. Good picks: Polythene, Rubber.
Needs to be absorbent. Good pick: Cotton cloth.
Needs to be stretchy and elastic. Good pick: Rubber.
Needs to be strong. Good picks: Cotton cloth, Jute.

items.f: A tiffin wrap for the rain
items.b: Needs to be waterproof. Good picks: Banana leaf, Foil, Polythene.

items.f: A rope to tie a boat
items.b: Needs to be strong. Good picks: Jute, Cotton cloth.

items.f: A cloth to wipe up spilt milk
items.b: Needs to be absorbent. Good picks: Paper napkin, Newspaper, Cotton cloth.
Needs to be strong and waterproof, and not bend or stretch. Good pick: Steel.
Needs to be very stretchy and elastic. Good pick: Rubber.

items.f: A scarf for a cold morning
items.b: Needs to be warm and soft. Good pick: Wool.
Stretchy and elastic. Waterproof.
Waterproof. Stretches and stays stretched.
Strong and absorbent. Not waterproof.
Absorbent and soft. Weak.
Absorbent. Hardly stretches.

img.credit: Kai Hendry from Singapore, Malaysia, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.b: Waterproof. Tears easily.
Waterproof. Soft and bendy.

img.credit: Karthik Thrikkadeeri, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Very strong and waterproof. Hard, does not stretch.
Strong. Absorbent.
Warm and soft. Soaks up water slowly. Stretches a little.

rules: Cut out the cards. Lay the 10 material cards face up in the middle of the table. Put the job cards face down in a pile.
Turn over the top job card and read the job aloud, but not the back.
On the count of three, every player points to one material card in the middle. Players may point to the same card.
Each player says in one sentence why that material works for the job.
Read the back of the job card. A player whose material is listed gets one point. If another material would really work and everyone agrees, that player gets one point too.
If players disagree, test it at home if you can.
After all 10 jobs, the player with the most points wins. If two players tie, they both win.

setup.art: Job cards in a pile, and material cards spread face up in the middle, with three players pointing at one.
setup.caption: 1. Job cards in a pile. Material cards face up in the middle.

setup.art: A child pointing at the 'Rubber' card next to a turned-over 'Hair band' job card.
setup.caption: 2. Point to a material for the job. Say why.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. Read each material card to your child. 3. Lay the material cards face up in the middle.
flow.say: Here are our materials. Some we tested ourselves. Listen to what each one is good at.
flow.kid: Look at your material cards. What is each one good at?

flow.do: 1. Turn over a job card and read it. 2. On the count of three, each player points to a material. 3. Each player says why. 4. Read the back and give points.
flow.say: The job is a raincoat. Count to three and point to the material you would pick. Why that one?
flow.kid: Read the job. Point to a material. Say why it works.

ask.q: Why did you pick that one?
good: Polythene, because it was waterproof in the spot test.

flow.parent: Give a point for any material that really works, even if it is not the one on the back. A steel raincoat is waterproof, but ask if it would bend.

flow.do: Ask your child which job was hardest to choose for, and why.
flow.say: Which job was the hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Which job was hardest? Why?

games.title: Stretch Line-up
games.context: This is a guessing game about stretchiness. Each player guesses the order of six things, from least stretchy to most stretchy. Then you test them and score points.

printables.title: 6 cards to cut out (one set for each player)
Score sheet
items: My order, from least stretchy (1) to most stretchy (6)
Points: one for each card in the right place

rules: Collect the six things on the cards. Cut out one set of six cards for each player.
Each player puts the six cards in a line on their score sheet, from least stretchy to most stretchy, without pulling anything.
Now test. One player holds each thing between two fingers of each hand, 5 cm apart, and pulls until it is hard to pull further.
Everyone watches and agrees an order.
Each player gets one point for every card in the right place.
The player with the most points wins. If two players tie, they both win.

setup.art: Six cards in a row on a score sheet, next to a rubber band, a sock, a hanky, a T-shirt strip, a newspaper strip and a hair band.
setup.caption: 1. Guess the order with the cards.

setup.art: A girl pulling a sock top between her fingers while two others watch.
setup.caption: 2. Test each one the same way.

flow.do: 1. Collect the six things. 2. Each player lines up their cards without touching the things.
flow.say: Without pulling anything, put the cards in order. Least stretchy first, most stretchy last.
flow.kid: Put the cards in order. Least stretchy first.
flow.parent: If your child cannot read the cards yet, put the real things in a line instead.

flow.do: 1. Test each thing by pulling it the same way, with fingers 5 cm apart. 2. Agree the order together.
flow.say: We must pull every one the same way. Why does that matter?
flow.kid: Pull each one the same way. Which stretched most?

ask.q: Why pull every one the same way?
good: So it is fair.
So only the material makes a difference.

flow.do: Score each player's line-up. Ask which guess surprised them.
flow.say: Which one surprised you? Why?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which one surprised you?

challenges.title: A Raincoat for a Paper Doll
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. You make a raincoat for a paper doll, using what your tests showed. Then you test it with water.
challenges.problem: Make a raincoat for a paper doll. Pour 3 teaspoons of water over the doll. When you take the raincoat off, the doll must still be dry.
constraints: Use at most 3 pieces of sticky tape.
The raincoat must come off without tearing the doll.
materials: a paper doll about 10 cm tall, cut from a notebook page and coloured with sketch pen
a milk packet, foil, a banana leaf, a polythene bag, newspaper and cloth scraps
a teaspoon, water and a tray
general: A coat cut from a milk packet or a polythene bag, taped at the shoulders.
A cape of foil folded round the doll.
creative: A hat and coat made from a banana leaf, like the palm-leaf umbrella called an olakkuda in Kerala.
A wide round hat that sheds water off its edge, like the japi hat of Assam, made of bamboo and palm leaves.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own raincoat. Test it with 3 teaspoons of water. If the doll gets wet, find where the water got in, and make it better.

setup.art: A paper doll coloured with sketch pen lying on a tray, next to a milk packet, foil and a banana leaf.
setup.caption: 1. Make and colour a paper doll.

setup.art: A child pouring water over a paper doll wearing a polythene coat.
setup.caption: 2. Put the raincoat on. Pour the water.

setup.art: A child taking off the coat to show a dry paper doll.
setup.caption: 3. Take it off. Is the doll dry?

flow.do: 1. Cut a paper doll from a notebook page. 2. Let your child colour it with sketch pen. 3. Read the challenge.
flow.say: The sketch pen will run if the doll gets wet. Which material will you use for the raincoat? Why?
flow.kid: Make a paper doll. Colour it. Which material will keep it dry? Why?

flow.do: Let your child make the raincoat. Help only with cutting.
flow.say: Remember the spot test. Which squares kept the water out?
flow.kid: Make the raincoat. Use what you found in the spot test.

flow.do: 1. Put the doll on the tray. 2. Pour 3 teaspoons of water slowly over the doll. 3. Take the raincoat off.
flow.say: Now the test. Is the doll dry? Where did any water get in?
flow.kid: Pour 3 spoons of water. Take the coat off. Is the doll dry?

ask.q: Where did the water get in?
good: At the neck.
Through the gap at the side.
Through the tape.

flow.parent: Water often gets in at the neck or the edges, even when the material is waterproof. This shows that the shape matters too.

flow.do: Ask your child to change one thing and test again.
flow.say: What will you change? Test it again.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: goes back after you stop pulling
items.why: These are the four property words we tested in this unit.

items.p: In the stretch test, which one usually stretches the most?
items.why: Rubber is made of long, curled-up chains that straighten when pulled. Newspaper hardly stretches at all.
items.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang the same full water bottle from a rubber band and from strips of T-shirt, hanky and newspaper, and measure how much longer each one gets.

items.p: Sort these into waterproof and not waterproof.
items.why: In the spot test, the circles under the foil, the leaf and the milk packet stayed dry. The others let water through.
items.context: This question is about the spot test. You pour a teaspoon of water on squares of different materials over paper marked with sketch pen, then lift each square to see if the water got through.

items.p: Draw the rubber band before the bottle, with the bottle, and after the bottle came off.
items.a: Three pictures: a short band, a long band with a bottle, and a short band again.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the band getting longer with the bottle and going back to the same length after. That is what elastic means.
items.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang the same full water bottle from a rubber band and from strips of T-shirt, hanky and newspaper, and measure how much longer each one gets.
items.art: Three empty boxes side by side, labelled before, with the bottle, after.

items.p: You can always tell if a material is waterproof just by looking at it.
items.why: False. A thick cotton towel may look as if it keeps water out, but it soaks water up. We have to test.

items.p: Deepa, a girl in Class 2, hangs a full bottle on the rubber band, and an empty cup on the T-shirt strip. Why is her stretch test not fair?
opts: The two strips hold different weights, so more than the material is different
The rubber band is too short
The cup is too small to see
items.why: For a fair test, every strip must hold the same weight. Then any difference in stretching comes from the material.
items.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang the same full water bottle from a rubber band and from strips of T-shirt, hanky and newspaper, and measure how much longer each one gets.

items.p: In the spot test, Fathima, a girl in Class 2, tested 6 squares. 3 circles stayed dry. How many circles ran?
items.why: 6 squares take away 3 dry ones leaves 3 that ran.
items.context: This question is about the spot test. You pour a teaspoon of water on squares of different materials over paper marked with sketch pen, then lift each square to see if the water got through.

items.p: Three of these spring back after you stretch them. Which one stays stretched?
items.why: The dough gets long and stays long. The other three are elastic, so they spring back.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: what happened to the milk packet strip when you pulled it and let go?
items.a: It got longer and thinner, went white in the middle, and stayed long.
items.why: A strong answer says both parts: it stretched, and it did not come back.

items.p: Label each picture: waterproof or absorbent.
items.why: An umbrella and a raincoat keep water out. A towel and a sponge soak it up.
items.art: Four small pictures with an empty label under each.

items.p: A material that soaks up water is called ____.
items.why: A towel, a napkin and a sponge are absorbent.

items.p: In the bottle lift, which strip usually tore first?
items.why: A napkin is made of short fibres pressed loosely together, so a small pull drags them apart. Picking the carry bag may mean thinking all plastic is weak. A carry bag strip holds much more than a napkin.
items.context: This question is about the bottle lift. You hang an empty bottle from a strip and add water one cup at a time until the strip tears.

items.p: Revathi and her brother Arun are buying a bag for vegetables.

views.says: Buy a cloth bag. It held the full bottle in our bottle lift, and we can use it for years.
Take a polythene bag. It is waterproof, so wet vegetables will not leak.

items.ask: Whose choice would you pick? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason from a test, such as 'the cloth held the full bottle'. It also says what the other is right about, such as 'polythene is waterproof'.
items.why: Both are partly right. The best material depends on what matters most for the job.

items.p: Draw something in your home that must be waterproof. Write what it is made of.
items.a: For example, an umbrella made of umbrella cloth, a bucket made of plastic, or a steel tumbler.
items.why: A strong answer names a real thing that needs to keep water in or out, and its material.
items.art: An empty box to draw in, with a line underneath for writing.

items.p: Match each job to the property it needs.
items.why: Each job needs a different property. No one material is best for all of them.

items.p: Look at the results. Which material did not get any longer with the bottle?
items.why: The hanky strip was 10 cm before and 10 cm with the bottle. The rubber band and the T-shirt strip both got longer.
items.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang the same full water bottle from a rubber band and from strips of T-shirt, hanky and newspaper, and measure how much longer each one gets.

items.p: Kavitha, a girl in Class 2, says, 'The T-shirt strip and the rubber band were both 13 cm with the bottle, so they stretch the same.' Is she right? Why?
items.a: No. The rubber band started at 6 cm and grew 7 cm. The T-shirt strip started at 10 cm and grew only 3 cm. So the rubber band stretched more.
items.why: A strong answer looks at how much each one grew, not only the final length.
items.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang the same full water bottle from a rubber band and from strips of T-shirt, hanky and newspaper, and measure how much longer each one gets.

items.p: Everything that stretches will spring back when you let go.
items.why: False. The milk packet strip and the atta dough stretched and stayed stretched.

items.p: Why does water soak through a cotton hanky?
opts: Cotton has tiny gaps between its fibres
items.why: Water creeps into the gaps between the fibres and spreads along them. Picking 'heavy' means mixing up weight with keeping water out.
items.context: This question is about the spot test. You pour a teaspoon of water on squares of different materials over paper marked with sketch pen, then lift each square to see if the water got through.

items.p: Put the steps of the stretch test in order.
items: Guess which will stretch most, and say why
Measure each strip with nothing on it
Hang the bottle and measure again
Take the bottle off and measure again
items.why: We guess first, so the test can check our guess. We measure before, so we can see how much each one changed.

items.p: Ishaan, a boy in Pune, tested two cloths, a hanky and a thick towel. He poured 1 spoon of water on the hanky and 3 spoons on the towel. More water got through the towel. Is his test fair? Why?
items.a: No. The towel got more water, so of course more got through. Each cloth needs the same amount of water.
items.why: A strong answer spots that two things changed: the cloth and the amount of water.

items.p: Sort these: springs back, or stays stretched?
items.why: Elastic materials spring back. Clay and milk packet plastic move into a new shape and stay there.

items.p: Draw what you think rubber looks like inside, when it is loose and when it is stretched.
items.a: Loose: curly, tangled lines. Stretched: the same lines pulled straighter.
items.why: Rubber is made of long, curled-up chains of tiny particles. Pulling straightens them. A strong drawing shows curled lines becoming straighter.
items.art: Two empty circles, labelled loose and stretched.

items.p: Pooja, a girl in Ahmedabad, needs a material for a catapult. What must it be?
items.why: A catapult band must stretch far and then snap back to throw. Picking 'strong and hard' would give a band that does not stretch.

items.p: A material that goes back to its old shape after you stop pulling is called ____.
items.why: A rubber band, a hair band and your skin are elastic.

items.p: Lakshmi and her grandmother are wrapping lunch for a picnic in the rain.

views.says: Use foil. It kept the circle dry in our spot test.
Use a banana leaf. It kept the water out too, and afterwards it goes back into the soil.

items.ask: Whose idea would you pick? Give one reason. Then say what the other one has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and uses a test result. Both were waterproof in the spot test. Paati also thinks about what happens to the wrap afterwards.
items.why: Both pass the waterproof test. Choosing between them depends on other things that matter too.

items.p: In the bottle lift, the napkin strip tore after 3 cups. The newspaper strip tore after 9 cups. How many more cups did the newspaper hold?
items.why: 9 take away 3 is 6. So the newspaper held 6 more cups than the napkin.
items.context: This question is about the bottle lift. You hang an empty bottle from a strip and add water one cup at a time until the strip tears.

items.p: Label the parts of the stretch test picture.
a: paper clip at the bottom of the band
items.why: Knowing each part helps you set up the test again.
items.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang the same full water bottle from a rubber band and from strips of T-shirt, hanky and newspaper, and measure how much longer each one gets.
items.art: A drawing of the stretch test set-up with five empty labels.

items.p: Some people say natural things like leaves and fibres are always weaker than things made in factories. Do you agree? Think of coir rope, which is made from coconut fibre.
items.a: No. Coir rope is made from coconut fibre and is strong enough to tie boats. Some natural things are strong and some are weak.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real example of a strong natural material and says that it depends on the material.

items.p: Your old hair band does not spring back any more. Why might that be? What could you test?
items.a: Old rubber, or rubber left in the sun, changes and stops being elastic. I could leave one new band in the sun and one in a drawer for a few weeks, and test which still springs back.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason and a fair test with one thing changed.

quiz.p: Hema, a girl in Class 2, hangs the same bottle from a rubber band and a hanky strip. Which stretches more?
quiz.why: Rubber is stretchy. Woven cotton hardly stretches. Picking 'both the same' may mean thinking all soft things stretch.

opts: It goes back after you stop pulling
quiz.why: Elastic things, like a rubber band, spring back. Picking 'soaks up water' mixes it up with absorbent.

quiz.p: Nila, a girl in Chennai, pulls a strip of milk packet and lets go. What happens?
quiz.why: The plastic in a milk packet stretches and stays stretched. Picking 'springs back' means thinking everything stretchy is elastic.

quiz.p: In the spot test, the circle under one square ran. What does that tell you?
quiz.why: The sketch pen runs only when water reaches it. So water got through. Picking 'waterproof' gets it the wrong way round.
Water stays on top of foil as a drop. Napkins and hankies soak it up.

quiz.p: Mary, a girl in Goa, hangs a bottle from strips and adds water one cup at a time. What is she testing?
quiz.why: Counting the cups before a strip tears shows how much weight it can hold. That is strength.

quiz.p: Why do we guess before we test?
opts: So the test can check our guess
So we don't need to test
quiz.why: A guess with a reason is an idea. The test shows if the idea was right. Picking 'so we don't need to test' skips the most important part.

quiz.p: A thicker cloth always keeps out more water.
quiz.why: False. A thick towel soaks up water. Thin polythene keeps it all out.

quiz.p: Which material would you choose for a towel?
quiz.why: A towel must soak up water. Cotton is absorbent. Polythene and foil are waterproof, so they would not dry you.

quiz.p: Harpreet, a girl in Ludhiana, tests strips with the same bottle. She waits 10 seconds for one strip and 5 minutes for another. Is it fair?
quiz.why: A strip may slowly stretch more over 5 minutes. Every strip should wait the same time.

applications: Raincoats, umbrellas and school bag covers are made of materials tested to be waterproof.
Hair bands, sock tops, pyjama waistbands and catapults use rubber because it is elastic.
Kerala grows most of India's natural rubber. Some of it becomes tyres, chappals and balloons.
Ropes, kite strings and shopping bags are tested to see how much weight they can hold.
Towels and nappies are made of absorbent materials.

open_questions.q: Why does rubber get old, cracked and stop springing back?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know sunlight, heat and air slowly break the long chains. But exactly how fast this happens in each kind of rubber is still being studied, so makers keep testing new ways to make rubber last.

open_questions.q: How do spiders make silk that is so strong and so stretchy at once?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have studied spider silk for many years. They still cannot make a material in a factory that is as good as the silk spiders make.

maths.problem: In the stretch test, the rubber band was 6 cm long. With the bottle it was 13 cm. How many centimetres longer did it get?
maths.explain: Count on from 6 to 13: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13. That is 7 steps. So the band got 7 cm longer.
maths.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang the same full water bottle from a rubber band and from strips of T-shirt, hanky and newspaper, and measure how much longer each one gets.
maths.why_maths: Taking the 'before' length away from the 'with the bottle' length tells us how much each one really stretched.

maths.problem: In the stretch test, the T-shirt strip was 10 cm long at the start. After the bottle came off it was 11 cm. How much longer than at the start was it?
maths.explain: 11 is more than 10. 11 take away 10 is 1. So the strip stayed 1 cm longer than it was at the start.
maths.context: This question is about the stretch test. You hang the same full water bottle from a rubber band and from strips of T-shirt, hanky and newspaper, and measure how much longer each one gets.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the start length with the end length shows that a strip can stay a little longer after the pull.

maths.problem: Bornali, a girl in Class 2, tested 8 squares in the spot test. 5 kept water out. How many let water through? Her friend Fathima found only 3 waterproof squares. Who found more waterproof squares, and how many more?
maths.answer: 3 let water through. Bornali found 2 more waterproof squares than Fathima.
maths.explain: 8 take away 5 is 3. 5 is more than 3, and 5 take away 3 is 2.
maths.context: This question is about the spot test. You pour a teaspoon of water on squares of different materials over paper marked with sketch pen, then lift each square to see if the water got through.
maths.why_maths: Counting and comparing the dry and wet squares helps us sum up a test in two numbers.

maths.problem: In the bottle lift, the napkin tore after 3 cups. Every cup holds 50 ml. How much water was in the bottle when it tore?
maths.explain: 3 cups of 50 ml: 50, 100, 150. So the napkin held 150 ml of water, as well as the bottle.
maths.context: This question is about the bottle lift. You hang an empty bottle from a strip and add water one cup at a time until the strip tears.
maths.why_maths: Turning cups into millilitres means anyone, anywhere, can repeat our test with the same amount of water.

maths.problem: Look at the chart from the bottle lift. Which strip held the most cups? Which held the fewest?
maths.answer: The cloth held the most, 10 cups, the full bottle. The napkin held the fewest, 3 cups.
maths.explain: The tallest bar is the cloth, at 10. The shortest bar is the napkin, at 3. The newspaper and the carry bag are in between.
maths.context: This question is about the bottle lift. You hang an empty bottle from a strip and add water one cup at a time until the strip tears.
maths.why_maths: A chart shows at a glance which material was strongest.

roots.context: We have tested which materials stretch, keep water out and hold weight. Now we ask what the stretch test tells us about materials, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Under the bottle, the rubber band stretched long, then went back to its old length. The milk packet strip we pulled stayed long and thin. Both stretched, yet only one came back. So to know a material, we must also watch what it does after the pull stops.
deep_truth.habit: We think 'stretchy' is one thing, and that a material we have stretched is the same afterwards. The test showed two stretchy materials doing opposite things once the pull stopped.
deep_truth.evidence: In the stretch test, the rubber band grew about 7 cm with the bottle and went back to its old length. The milk packet strip, pulled by hand, got thin and white and stayed long. Inside rubber, long curled chains straighten and curl back. In the plastic, the chains slide to new places and stay.

three.who_am_i: Your skin is elastic. You bend your knee, and the skin stretches. You straighten it, and the skin goes back.
three.what_is_life: A rubber tree makes latex, and latex seals a cut in the bark. Living things make the materials they need.
three.what_is_this_world: Every material does something different when it is pulled, wetted or loaded. We only find out by testing.

roots.thread: Rubber, cotton, paper and polythene are all made of tiny particles, joined in different ways. Long curled chains let rubber spring back. Short, loose fibres let a napkin tear. Everything is conscious, the rubber tree too. When the tree is cut, latex flows out and dries to seal the cut.

teachings.teaching: Whatever you hear, and whoever says it, wisdom is seeing what is really true in it.
teachings.link: A shopkeeper may say a bag is the strongest. The Tirukkural, from Tamil Nadu, asks us to find out what is true. A fair test is one way to do that.

teachings.teaching: Nothing in the world is softer than water. Yet nothing is better at wearing away what is hard and strong.
teachings.link: In the spot test, soft water found its way through paper and cloth. Only materials with no gaps kept it out.

teachings.source: Jain teaching of anekantavada, many-sidedness, and the story of the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Each blind man touched one part of the elephant and thought he knew the whole animal. Each was partly right.
teachings.link: Each of our tests showed one side of a material. Milk packet plastic kept water out, but it stayed stretched and did not go back. To know a material, we need many tests.

science.text: Rubber is made of very long chains of tiny particles. Stretching straightens the chains, and they curl back when let go. This is why rubber is elastic.
Weight for weight, spider silk is one of the strongest materials known. Scientists are still trying to make a material as good in a factory.

other_view.view: They explain a rubber band without any mind. The chains are always jiggling, and jiggling chains tend to settle in curled shapes, so a stretched band is pulled back. They do not use awareness to explain it.

practice.title: Stretch and come back
practice.say: Stand up tall. Stretch your arms up high, as far as they go. Feel your body get longer. Hold it. Now let go, slowly. Feel your arms come back to your sides. Breathe in slowly, and your chest gets bigger. Breathe out, and it goes back. Your body stretches and comes back all day long.
practice.kid: Stand up. Stretch your arms up high. Hold it. Now let go slowly. Breathe in. Your chest gets bigger. Breathe out. It goes back.

science: Rubber elasticity: natural rubber is cis-polyisoprene, long chain molecules that are coiled at rest and straighten under stretching (entropic elasticity). Any polymer science textbook.
Polyethylene (milk packet film) yields and necks under tension and does not recover, because its chains slide and reorient (plastic deformation).
Natural rubber in India: Hevea brasiliensis is tapped in Kerala, where most of India's natural rubber is grown (Rubber Board of India).
D. Hosler, S. L. Burkett and M. J. Tarkanian, 'Prehistoric Polymers: Rubber Processing in Ancient Mesoamerica', Science 284 (1999), 1988-1991. Rubber balls from El Manati, Mexico, about 1600 BCE.

M. J. Tarkanian and D. Hosler, 'America's First Polymer Scientists: Rubber Processing, Use and Transport in Mesoamerica', Latin American Antiquity 22 (2011): different mixes of latex and morning glory juice for different uses.
Charles Goodyear, vulcanisation of rubber with sulfur and heat, 1839, patented 1844.
Spider dragline silk: very strong for the weight of the silk, and very tough (for example, Gosline and others, Journal of Experimental Biology, 1999).
sources.walkthrough: Every test was walked through for a city flat. A full half-litre bottle weighs about half a kilogram. That is enough to stretch an ordinary rubber band to about double, and a knitted T-shirt strip cut across the shirt by a few centimetres. It is far too little to stretch or tear a 2 cm strip of woven cotton or newspaper. The milk packet strip is pulled by hand, because a bottle may not be heavy enough to stretch thick polythene, while a thin milk or bread packet strip 1 cm wide stretches and whitens easily in a child's hands. In the spot test, water-based sketch pen runs as soon as it is wet, so a wet paper is easy to see. In the bottle lift, a 1 cm strip of one layer of paper napkin usually tears with a few small cups of water, while 1 cm strips of newspaper and cotton usually hold the full bottle; a strip of a thick carry bag may hold it or may stretch a lot. Results vary from home to home, and that is fine. The spine is the stretch test after the intro (session 1, about 30 minutes), then the explanations, Roots, the spot test and the quiz (session 2, about 40 minutes).

playtest: Walked the unit as a parent and child in a flat: stretch test, spot test, bottle lift, both games and the raincoat challenge, with minutes, steps and schedules checked. Fixed: the job-and-material game now works with 2 and 4 players with all 20 cards written out; the line-up game says one card set per player; the choose-a-material activity repeated the game, so it has new jobs; the spot test now pours and lifts at one timing and lists the sketch pen; repeated maths and worksheet questions replaced; names introduced; cards shortened; weak jokes, unchecked video placeholders and the unneeded ruler purchase removed.
